title: Teaching Multiple Strands at Once
author: Dylan Kane
summary: Dylan Kane describes adopting a 'strands' model of lesson planning, borrowed loosely from the Direct Instruction concept of 'tracks', where a single lesson works on several different, not-necessarily-connected topics rather than one unifying theme. Rather than fully committing to the ambitious multi-track structure he saw in a Direct Instruction programme spanning 120 lessons, Kane describes a lighter version: his units still exist, but blend into each other at the edges, introducing next-unit skills in the final weeks of a current unit while continuing to practise key skills from the unit before. He lists five concrete benefits: more time to gradually escalate difficulty across days rather than within one lesson, a built-in 'slow start' preview at the beginning of each unit, natural interleaving and spaced practice, protection against a single bad lesson consuming the whole class period, and better-paced repetitive practice that avoids students switching off. He closes with practical starting steps for teachers curious about trying the approach, beginning with a low-stakes previous-lesson check for understanding via mini-whiteboards.
points: Kane's core structural move -- replacing 'one lesson, one objective' with several parallel, less-connected 'strands' -- borrows directly from Direct Instruction's 'tracks' model while explicitly avoiding a full adoption of that program's more rigid structure.

His 'slow start' unit design (previewing next-unit skills in the final weeks of the current unit) builds an assessment-and-preview function directly into the curriculum sequence rather than relying on a single diagnostic pre-test.

The claim that strands protect against a bad lesson 'blowing up' the whole period -- since only one strand fails, not the entire lesson -- is a specific resilience argument for multi-strand lesson design that single-objective lessons don't offer.

His observation that 'practice that's too repetitive... leads students to stop thinking' links the strands approach directly to interleaving and spaced-practice research, positioning it as cognitive-science-aligned rather than just a scheduling convenience.
quotes: One change I've made in my teaching this year is teaching multiple "strands" of content in a single lesson.
The idea of multiple strands comes from the Direct Instruction program. DI calls them "tracks" but that word has another meaning so I call them strands.
In any individual lesson there are chunks of time working on a few different strands, not necessarily connected to each other. Lessons don’t have a single objective.
I have more time to gradually increase the difficulty of a skill. Rather than increasing the difficulty within a single lesson I am often gradually increasing the difficulty over multiple days.
I don't put all my eggs in one basket for a lesson. I've taught lots of lessons in my career where I realize early on it's not going to go well, but I don’t have anything else planned and I plow on.
Practice is important, but practice that's too repetitive usually leads students to stop thinking. Lots of small chunks of focused practice work better.
